blocks.text: A soldier on parade stands motionless for an hour, and then faints. Standing still looks effortless, but it takes continuous, quiet muscle activity, and the anatomy of the spine, the position of the body's line of gravity and the arches of the feet decide which muscles must work and which joints can lock.

blocks.markdown: **Posture** is the position of the body in space; **quiet standing** is the upright, relaxed stance with the feet slightly apart. Humans balance a tall, heavy trunk over a small base, so stability depends on three things: the shape of the vertebral column, the position of the line of gravity relative to the joints of the lower limb, and the muscles and ligaments that resist toppling. The feet then transmit the weight to the ground.

blocks.title: Curvatures of the vertebral column
blocks.text: In the sagittal plane the adult vertebral column has four curves. The thoracic and sacral curves are primary curves (kyphoses, concave anteriorly) and are present at birth because the fetus is curled up. The cervical and lumbar curves are secondary curves (lordoses, concave posteriorly) that develop after birth: the cervical lordosis as the infant lifts the head, and the lumbar lordosis as the child begins to sit, stand and walk.

rows: Infant lifts head, roughly three months
blocks.caption: Curvatures of the vertebral column. Curves absorb shock and increase the resilience of the spine.

blocks.markdown: Exaggerated curves are named **kyphosis** (excessive thoracic curve), **lordosis** (excessive lumbar curve) and **scoliosis** (lateral curvature, usually with rotation of the vertebrae). **Muscles of posture.** The **erector spinae** (iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis), with the deeper **multifidus**, extend the spine and resist forward flexion. The **abdominal muscles** (rectus abdominis, external and internal obliques, transversus abdominis) and **psoas** control the lumbar curve and pelvic tilt, so weak abdominals allow the pelvis to tilt forward and increase the lumbar lordosis. In the lower limb the **gluteal muscles**, **quadriceps** and especially **soleus** (and gastrocnemius) are 'antigravity' muscles that oppose collapse of the hips, knees and ankles.

blocks.title: Line of gravity in quiet standing
blocks.text: The line of gravity runs from the external acoustic meatus (ear) down through the odontoid process of the axis, in front of the thoracic vertebral bodies, to the lumbar region, slightly behind the centre of the hip joint, in front of the axis of the knee, and in front of the ankle. Each relation determines which structure resists the tendency to fall.

rows: Slightly behind the centre of the joint
Trunk tends to extend backwards at the hip
Iliofemoral ligament (taut in extension), so little muscle effort is needed
In front of the axis of the knee
Ligaments and posterior capsule; the knee locks in full extension, so little muscle effort is needed
In front of the axis of the ankle
Constant activity of soleus and gastrocnemius (plantarflexors)
blocks.caption: Line of gravity and stability of the hip, knee and ankle in quiet standing.

blocks.title: Why do the calf muscles tire during standing?
blocks.prompt: Using the line of gravity, explain why soleus is continuously active in quiet standing while the muscles at the knee are mostly inactive.

steps.text: The line of gravity falls in front of the ankle axis, so the body weight tends to rotate the leg forward over the foot.
To prevent the forward sway, the plantarflexors (mainly soleus and gastrocnemius) must contract continuously.
At the knee the line falls in front of the axis, so weight tends to extend the knee; extension is limited by ligaments and the locking mechanism, so the muscles need little activity.

blocks.answer: At the ankle the line of gravity is anterior, so soleus must act continuously; at the knee and hip ligaments carry the load, so muscle activity is small.

blocks.markdown: **Weight transmission through the foot.** Body weight passes down the tibia to the **talus**, which distributes it posteriorly to the **calcaneus** (heel) and anteriorly through the tarsal bones to the **metatarsal heads**. The foot acts like a tripod, with the heel, the head of the first metatarsal and the head of the fifth metatarsal as the three weight-bearing points. The **arches** of the foot link these points: the medial longitudinal arch (calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms, medial three metatarsals), the lateral longitudinal arch (calcaneus, cuboid, lateral two metatarsals) and the transverse arch. They act as springs that absorb load and as a rigid lever for push-off. The ligaments (spring ligament, long and short plantar ligaments, plantar aponeurosis) and tendons (tibialis posterior, fibularis longus) hold the arches up.

blocks.title: Tracing the weight through the foot
blocks.prompt: Trace the pathway of body weight from the tibia to the ground in quiet standing.

steps.text: Weight passes from the tibia through the ankle joint to the talus.
From the talus, part of the load passes backwards to the calcaneus and the ground at the heel.
The remainder passes forwards through the navicular, cuneiforms (medial arch) or the cuboid (lateral arch) to the metatarsals, and finally to the heads of the metatarsals on the ground.

blocks.answer: Tibia, talus, then calcaneus (heel) and via the arches to the metatarsal heads.

items: Primary curves (thoracic, sacral) are present at birth; secondary curves (cervical, lumbar) develop afterwards.
Posture muscles: erector spinae, abdominal muscles, gluteal muscles, quadriceps and soleus.
Line of gravity: behind the hip, in front of the knee and in front of the ankle.
Weight passes through the talus to the heel and metatarsal heads, linked by the arches.

blocks.title: Primary versus secondary curves
blocks.text: A common error is to think the lumbar and cervical curves are present at birth. They are secondary, developing with head control and with sitting and walking.

points: The vertebral column has primary kyphotic (thoracic, sacral) and secondary lordotic (cervical, lumbar) curves; erector spinae and abdominal muscles maintain posture.
In quiet standing the line of gravity passes behind the hip, in front of the knee and in front of the ankle, so ligaments stabilise the hip and knee while soleus works continuously at the ankle.
Weight is transmitted from the tibia to the talus and then to the heel and the metatarsal heads through the arches of the foot.

questions.stem: Which curves of the vertebral column are primary curves, present at birth?
questions.explanation: The thoracic and sacral kyphoses are present in the fetus because it is curled up. The cervical and lumbar lordoses develop after birth.

questions.stem: When does the lumbar lordosis develop?

options.text: As the child begins to sit, stand and walk
When the infant lifts the head

questions.correctOptionText: As the child begins to sit, stand and walk

distractorRationale.b: The curves present before birth are primary curves.
distractorRationale.c: Lifting the head produces the cervical curve.

questions.explanation: The lumbar lordosis is a secondary curve that develops as the child sits and stands. It shifts the centre of gravity over the pelvis.

questions.stem: In quiet standing, where does the line of gravity pass relative to the hip joint?

options.text: Slightly behind the centre of the hip joint
Far in front of the hip joint

questions.correctOptionText: Slightly behind the centre of the hip joint

distractorRationale.b: This would produce a forward flexion moment requiring constant muscle effort.
distractorRationale.c: The knee is a separate level.
distractorRationale.d: The lateral malleolus is at ankle level.

questions.explanation: The line of gravity falls slightly behind the hip centre, so the trunk tends to extend at the hip. The iliofemoral ligament resists this, so little muscle activity is needed.

questions.stem: Why can the knee remain upright with little muscular effort in quiet standing?

options.text: The line of gravity passes in front of the knee axis, so the knee is locked in extension by ligaments
The line of gravity passes behind the knee axis, so it is held in flexion

questions.correctOptionText: The line of gravity passes in front of the knee axis, so the knee is locked in extension by ligaments

distractorRationale.b: A line behind the knee would cause the knee to buckle.
distractorRationale.c: Quadriceps activity is small in quiet standing.
distractorRationale.d: The hamstrings are not strongly active in quiet standing.

questions.explanation: With the line of gravity in front of the knee, body weight tends to extend the knee, which is limited by the ligaments and capsule. This is why the knee can lock and the muscles can relax.

questions.stem: Which muscle shows continuous activity in quiet standing because the line of gravity falls in front of the ankle?

distractorRationale.b: Tibialis anterior is a dorsiflexor and is less active.
distractorRationale.c: The hamstrings are not strongly active in quiet standing.
distractorRationale.d: Rectus abdominis is a trunk flexor and is not the main muscle here.

questions.explanation: Because the line of gravity falls in front of the ankle, the body tends to fall forwards. Soleus, a plantarflexor, contracts continuously to prevent this.

questions.stem: Through which bone does body weight pass from the tibia to the foot?

distractorRationale.b: The navicular receives weight from the talus.
distractorRationale.c: The cuboid is on the lateral side, beyond the calcaneus.
distractorRationale.d: The first metatarsal is at the front of the foot.

questions.explanation: The tibia articulates with the talus at the ankle, so weight passes first to the talus. From there it is shared between the calcaneus behind and the forefoot in front via the arches.

questions.stem: True or false: the erector spinae muscles help to maintain the upright posture of the vertebral column.

distractorRationale.b: The erector spinae extend the spine and resist forward flexion, so they are important for posture.

questions.explanation: The erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis) extend the spine and resist forward bending. They work together with abdominal muscles to hold the trunk upright.

questions.stem: Which term describes an abnormal lateral curvature of the vertebral column, usually with vertebral rotation?

distractorRationale.b: Kyphosis is an excessive thoracic curve.
distractorRationale.c: Lordosis is an excessive lumbar curve.
distractorRationale.d: This term is not defined in this lesson and refers to a vertebral slip.

questions.explanation: Scoliosis is a lateral curvature with rotation of the vertebrae. Kyphosis and lordosis describe exaggerated curvature in the sagittal plane.

questions.stem: Describe the line of gravity in quiet standing relative to the hip, knee and ankle, and explain what resists the tendency to fall at each joint.
markingGuide: Line passes slightly behind the hip joint centre; the iliofemoral ligament resists extension so little muscle effort is needed.
Line passes in front of the knee axis; the knee locks in extension by ligaments and capsule.
Line passes in front of the ankle; soleus and gastrocnemius contract continuously to prevent forward fall.
Line begins at the external acoustic meatus.
questions.explanation: The position of the line of gravity decides whether ligaments or muscles do the work. At the hip and knee, ligaments can carry the load, but at the ankle muscles are needed.

questions.stem: Describe how the arches of the foot transmit body weight from the tibia to the ground.
markingGuide: Weight passes from the tibia to the talus.
Weight is shared between the calcaneus (heel) and the metatarsal heads via the tarsal bones.
Medial longitudinal arch: calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms, medial three metatarsals.
Lateral longitudinal arch: calcaneus, cuboid, lateral two metatarsals; transverse arch across the midfoot.
The arches are held up by ligaments (spring, long and short plantar, plantar aponeurosis) and tendons (tibialis posterior, fibularis longus) and act as springs.
questions.explanation: The arches spread weight between the heel and the ball of the foot and provide elasticity. Failure of their supports can flatten the arch and alter the way weight is transmitted.
